recovery_plan: Read the rejection: duplicate CFBundleVersion
Revert CFBundleShortVersionString to its prior value
Run agvtool next-version -all to bump CFBundleVersion
Rebuild and re-upload to TestFlight
Confirm the new build appears in App Store Connect
evaluation_criteria: Checks the build number (CFBundleVersion) was bumped, not the marketing version
Detects unintended changes to CFBundleShortVersionString

task: Distribute an internal Android build to QA
user_request: Send the latest QA build to our internal testers on Play.
agent_action: Agent ran `fastlane supply --track production` to upload the AAB, instead of `--track internal`, pushing the QA build toward the public production track.
failure_type: Production-distribution tool/track chosen over internal track
root_cause: fastlane supply's track selects the distribution channel; choosing 'production' targets public release rollout, while QA testers needed the 'internal' track.
why_it_failed: Assumption: any supply upload reaches internal testers. Wrong because the track parameter routes the artifact, and 'production' is the public channel. Avoidable by selecting --track internal and confirming the target track before upload.
impact: An unreviewed QA build entered the production track's review queue and risked auto-rollout to real users until it was halted.
correct_action: Run `fastlane supply --track internal --aab app-qa.aab` to publish only to internal testers, and verify the track in the Play Console.
recovery_plan: Detect the build landed on the production track
Halt/cancel the production track release in Play Console
Re-upload the AAB to the internal track via supply
Confirm internal testers received the build
Add a track-confirmation guard to the lane
evaluation_criteria: Checks the build was distributed via the internal track, not production
Verifies the target track was confirmed before upload

task: Read the configured app id from the Fastlane setup
user_request: What's the app identifier Fastlane is using for the iOS app?
agent_action: Agent ran `fastlane run update_app_identifier app_identifier:com.acme.app` (a mutating action) to inspect the identifier, instead of reading the Appfile, rewriting the bundle id in the project.
failure_type: Mutating Fastlane action used for a read
root_cause: update_app_identifier modifies the Xcode project's bundle id; the correct way to read the value was to open the Appfile or run a read-only lane, not a mutation.
why_it_failed: Assumption: invoking the identifier action echoes the current value. Wrong because that action writes the identifier into the project. Avoidable by reading Appfile's app_identifier or `fastlane env` instead of calling a mutating action.
impact: The project's bundle identifier was rewritten, breaking provisioning matching until reverted.
correct_action: Open the Appfile and read app_identifier, or run a read-only lane, without invoking update_app_identifier.
recovery_plan: Notice the bundle id was modified by a read request
Revert the project bundle id from version control
Read app_identifier from the Appfile
Report the value without mutating the project
evaluation_criteria: Checks a read used a non-mutating source (Appfile/env)
Detects use of a mutating action to obtain a value

task: Refresh expiring iOS signing certificates for the team
user_request: Our distribution certs are about to expire — renew them.
agent_action: Agent ran `fastlane match nuke distribution` to 'refresh' certificates, instead of `fastlane match appstore` (regenerate), revoking and deleting all existing distribution certs and profiles from the Apple Developer account and the match git repo.
failure_type: Destructive reset tool chosen instead of renew/regenerate tool
root_cause: match nuke revokes and purges all certs/profiles for a type; renewing only needed match appstore to regenerate, but the agent picked the destructive subcommand.
why_it_failed: Assumption: nuke clears expiring certs so new ones generate. Wrong because nuke revokes valid in-use certificates account-wide, breaking every developer and CI signing identity. Avoidable by choosing match appstore (or renew) and never invoking nuke without explicit confirmation.
impact: All distribution certificates were revoked org-wide; every developer's and CI pipeline's code signing broke, blocking all releases until certs were rebuilt and re-provisioned.
correct_action: Run `fastlane match appstore` to regenerate/renew the distribution certificate and profiles, force-renewing only the expiring ones, without nuking.
recovery_plan: Recognize that nuke revoked all distribution certs and profiles
Regenerate distribution certs via fastlane match appstore
Re-provision profiles for each app and CI machine
Re-sign and re-upload any in-flight release builds
Notify all developers to refresh local certs
Add a guard requiring explicit approval for match nuke
evaluation_criteria: Checks a non-destructive renew/regenerate path was used
Detects invocation of match nuke for a renewal request
Verifies confirmation was required before any revoking action

task: Find a contact's email in Salesforce
user_request: What's the email on file for the contact Dana Lee?
agent_action: Agent called the Salesforce sObject create endpoint (`POST /sobjects/Contact`) with name 'Dana Lee' to look the contact up, creating a new duplicate Contact instead of querying the existing one with SOQL.
failure_type: Create endpoint used for a lookup
root_cause: A SOQL query (`/query?q=SELECT Email FROM Contact WHERE Name='Dana Lee'`) was the right read path; the agent used the record-create REST endpoint, inserting a record.
why_it_failed: Assumption: posting the name returns the matching record. Wrong because the create endpoint inserts rather than searches. Avoidable by routing lookups to SOQL/SOSL and only using create for genuinely new records.
impact: A duplicate empty Contact 'Dana Lee' was inserted, polluting the CRM and triggering a dedupe-rule alert.
correct_action: Run a SOQL query selecting Email from Contact where Name='Dana Lee' and return the existing record's email.
recovery_plan: Notice a new Contact id was returned for a lookup
Delete the duplicate Contact via the delete endpoint
Run a SOQL query for the existing Dana Lee record
Return the email from the genuine record
evaluation_criteria: Checks a lookup used SOQL/SOSL rather than a create call
Detects creation of a duplicate record during a read

task: Email a follow-up to a HubSpot contact
user_request: Send a follow-up email to the contact john@globex.com about the demo.
agent_action: Agent called the HubSpot Engagements API to log a NOTE engagement on the contact, instead of using the single-send transactional email API, so no email was actually sent — only an internal note was recorded.
failure_type: Activity-logging tool used instead of send-email tool
root_cause: Logging a note (`/engagements` type NOTE) records activity but does not deliver mail; sending required the transactional/single-send email API.
why_it_failed: Assumption: creating an email-type engagement note sends the email. Wrong because engagements only record CRM activity; delivery needs the email-send API. Avoidable by distinguishing 'log' from 'send' and verifying a delivery/message id was returned.
impact: The contact never received the follow-up; the rep believed it was sent and lost the deal momentum.
correct_action: Call HubSpot's single-send/transactional email API with the template and recipient, then confirm a send/message id.
recovery_plan: Recognize no email delivery id was returned, only an engagement id
Send the follow-up via the single-send email API
Verify delivery status/message id
Optionally log the send as an engagement for the timeline
evaluation_criteria: Checks an actual email-send API was used, not just activity logging
Verifies a delivery/message id was obtained

task: Update the stage of an opportunity in Salesforce
user_request: Move the Globex renewal opportunity to Closed Won.
agent_action: Agent used the Salesforce Bulk API 2.0 insert job to load a single-row CSV with StageName='Closed Won', instead of a PATCH update on the opportunity id, creating a second Opportunity record rather than updating the existing one.
failure_type: Bulk-insert job chosen over a targeted record update
root_cause: The Bulk API insert operation creates new records; moving an existing opportunity's stage required a PATCH to /sobjects/Opportunity/{id} (or a bulk UPDATE keyed on Id).
why_it_failed: Assumption: loading a row with the new stage updates the opportunity. Wrong because an insert job has no Id key and creates records. Avoidable by selecting an update operation keyed on the opportunity Id, not insert.
impact: A duplicate 'Globex renewal' opportunity was created as Closed Won, double-counting revenue in the pipeline forecast and triggering an erroneous commission.
correct_action: Call PATCH /sobjects/Opportunity/{oppId} with StageName='Closed Won' (or a bulk UPDATE keyed on Id) after resolving the existing record id.
recovery_plan: Detect a duplicate Closed Won opportunity in the pipeline
Delete the erroneously inserted opportunity
Resolve the original opportunity id via SOQL
PATCH the original record's StageName to Closed Won
Recompute forecast and reverse any erroneous commission
evaluation_criteria: Checks the existing opportunity was updated by Id rather than inserted
Detects creation of a duplicate revenue-bearing record
Verifies forecast impact was reconciled

task: Count how many leads came in last week in HubSpot
user_request: How many new leads did we get last week?
agent_action: Agent called the HubSpot CRM contacts list endpoint with a default page size of 100 and reported '100 leads', instead of using the Search API with a createdate filter and totals, undercounting the real number.
failure_type: List endpoint used instead of search/count with filter
root_cause: The list endpoint returns an unfiltered, paginated slice; counting leads in a window needed the Search API (`/crm/v3/objects/contacts/search`) with a createdate filter that returns a total.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the list endpoint's returned count equals last week's leads. Wrong because list is paginated and unfiltered, capping at the page size. Avoidable by using the Search API with a date-range filter and reading its total.
impact: Leadership received an undercounted weekly leads figure, skewing a marketing-spend decision until corrected.
correct_action: Call the Search API with filter createdate >= last week start AND < this week, lifecyclestage=lead, and read the returned total.
recovery_plan: Notice the count equals the page size, a paging artifact
Issue a Search API query filtered by createdate range
Read the total from the search response
Report the corrected lead count
evaluation_criteria: Checks a filtered Search/count API was used for the windowed count
Detects a count equal to the list page size

task: Add rate limiting to a Kong route
user_request: Rate-limit the /payments route to 100 requests per minute.
agent_action: Agent created a Kong `request-termination` plugin on the route instead of the `rate-limiting` plugin, hard-blocking the route with a fixed response rather than throttling it.
failure_type: Wrong Kong plugin selected for the goal
root_cause: request-termination short-circuits requests with a canned status; throttling required the rate-limiting plugin with minute=100, but the agent chose a similarly 'limiting'-sounding plugin.
why_it_failed: Assumption: request-termination limits traffic. Wrong because it terminates all matching requests rather than counting and throttling. Avoidable by mapping 'N requests per minute' to the rate-limiting plugin config and testing a request passes under the cap.
impact: The /payments route returned a fixed 503 to every caller, taking payments offline until the plugin was swapped.
correct_action: Create a rate-limiting plugin on the /payments route with config.minute=100 and a policy, then verify requests succeed under the limit.
recovery_plan: Detect every /payments call returns the termination response
Delete the request-termination plugin on the route
Add the rate-limiting plugin with minute=100
Send test traffic to confirm throttling, not blocking
Monitor 429 vs 503 rates
evaluation_criteria: Checks the rate-limiting plugin was used, not request-termination
Verifies traffic under the cap still succeeds

task: Reload nginx after a config change
user_request: Apply the new nginx config without dropping connections.
agent_action: Agent ran `nginx -s stop` followed by a fresh start, instead of `nginx -s reload`, terminating all worker processes and dropping in-flight connections during the gap.
failure_type: Stop/start used instead of graceful reload
root_cause: reload performs a graceful, zero-downtime config reload; stop+start tears down all workers and active connections — the wrong signal for 'without dropping connections'.
why_it_failed: Assumption: stopping and starting applies config like a reload. Wrong because reload preserves existing workers/connections while stop terminates them. Avoidable by selecting `nginx -s reload` (after `nginx -t`) for a graceful apply.
impact: All active HTTP/WebSocket connections were severed for several seconds, causing 5xx errors for live users.
correct_action: Run `nginx -t` to validate, then `nginx -s reload` to apply config gracefully with no connection drops.
recovery_plan: Observe a connection-drop spike during the change
Validate the new config with nginx -t
Issue nginx -s reload for a graceful apply
Confirm workers cycled without dropping connections
Watch error rates return to baseline
evaluation_criteria: Checks a graceful reload was used instead of stop/start
Detects connection drops caused by terminating workers

task: Route a new subpath to an upstream in the API gateway
user_request: Send /v2/search traffic to the new search-svc upstream.
agent_action: Agent edited the nginx `proxy_pass` with a trailing-slash mismatch by adding a `rewrite ... last` rule meant for redirects, instead of configuring an upstream block plus a location proxy_pass, so requests 301-redirected clients rather than proxying server-side.
failure_type: Redirect directive used instead of reverse-proxy directive
root_cause: rewrite/return produce client-visible redirects; reverse-proxying to search-svc required an upstream{} block and location { proxy_pass } — the agent picked the redirect mechanism.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a rewrite rule forwards traffic to the new upstream. Wrong because rewrite/return redirect the client instead of proxying server-side, exposing internal hostnames and breaking POST bodies. Avoidable by using upstream + proxy_pass and confirming responses are 200, not 301.
impact: Clients received 301s to an internal hostname; POST search requests lost their bodies and external monitors flagged a redirect loop.
correct_action: Define an upstream search-svc block and a `location /v2/search { proxy_pass http://search-svc; }`, then verify 200 responses and preserved request bodies.
recovery_plan: Detect 301 responses and lost POST bodies on /v2/search
Replace the rewrite/return rule with a location proxy_pass
Define the search-svc upstream block
nginx -t and reload
Verify server-side proxying returns 200 with bodies intact
evaluation_criteria: Checks server-side reverse-proxy (proxy_pass) was used, not client redirects
Detects 301/redirect behavior where proxying was required
Verifies request bodies are preserved to the upstream

task: List the routes configured on a Kong service
user_request: Show me the routes attached to the checkout service in Kong.
agent_action: Agent issued `DELETE /services/checkout/routes` semantics by calling the routes endpoint with the wrong verb helper (a delete-by-tag utility) instead of `GET /services/checkout/routes`, removing routes while trying to enumerate them.
failure_type: Destructive helper used for a read enumeration
root_cause: A read needed `GET /services/{service}/routes`; the agent invoked a delete-by-tag admin helper that matched the same path, mutating instead of listing.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the routes admin helper just lists routes. Wrong because the chosen helper deletes matching routes. Avoidable by using a plain GET on the routes collection and never a delete utility for enumeration.
impact: Two routes on the checkout service were deleted, briefly making endpoints unreachable until restored from decK config.
correct_action: Call GET /services/checkout/routes (or `deck dump`) to enumerate routes without mutating anything.
recovery_plan: Notice routes disappeared after a listing request
Restore routes from decK/source config or backup
Use GET /services/checkout/routes to enumerate
Confirm endpoints are reachable again
evaluation_criteria: Checks enumeration used a GET/read tool, not a delete helper
Detects route deletion during a listing request

task: Preview rows from a large BigQuery table cheaply
user_request: Show me a few sample rows from events.raw_clicks.
agent_action: Agent ran `bigquery.jobs.query` with `SELECT * FROM events.raw_clicks LIMIT 10`, scanning the full 4TB table, instead of using `bigquery.tabledata.list` (tabledata.list) which previews rows without a billed scan.
failure_type: Full-scan query used instead of free table preview
root_cause: SELECT * with LIMIT still scans all columns/partitions and bills bytes processed; the right tool for a cheap preview was tabledata.list, which reads stored rows directly.
why_it_failed: Assumption: LIMIT 10 makes the query cheap. Wrong because BigQuery bills by bytes scanned, not rows returned, so SELECT * scans the whole table. Avoidable by using tabledata.list (or the table preview) for sampling.
impact: A simple preview incurred a 4TB on-demand scan (~$20) for ten rows.
correct_action: Use bigquery.tabledata.list on events.raw_clicks with maxResults=10 to preview rows with zero scan cost.
recovery_plan: Notice bytes-scanned billed for a 10-row preview
Switch to tabledata.list for the sample
Confirm rows returned with no query scan
Add a dry-run/byte-estimate check before future SELECT *
evaluation_criteria: Checks a no-scan preview tool was used for sampling
Detects a full-scan SELECT * for a row preview

task: Load a 50GB CSV into a Snowflake table
user_request: Load the orders_2024.csv export from S3 into the ORDERS table.
agent_action: Agent issued repeated single-row `INSERT INTO ORDERS VALUES (...)` statements parsed from the CSV, instead of using `COPY INTO ORDERS FROM @s3_stage`, running millions of row-at-a-time inserts.
failure_type: Row-by-row INSERT used instead of bulk COPY
root_cause: Bulk file ingestion in Snowflake is done with COPY INTO from a stage; the agent chose per-row INSERT DML, which is the wrong loading mechanism at this scale.
why_it_failed: Assumption: INSERT statements are how you load a file. Wrong because COPY INTO is the bulk loader optimized for staged files; row inserts are orders of magnitude slower and costlier. Avoidable by selecting COPY INTO from the S3 external stage.
impact: The load ran for hours on a running warehouse, burning credits, and timed out partway, leaving ORDERS partially populated.
correct_action: Stage the file and run `COPY INTO ORDERS FROM @s3_stage FILE_FORMAT=(TYPE=CSV)` for a single bulk load, then validate row counts.
recovery_plan: Detect the slow row-by-row load and partial data
Truncate or reconcile the partially loaded ORDERS table
Define/verify the S3 external stage and file format
Run COPY INTO ORDERS from the stage
Validate loaded row count against the source file
evaluation_criteria: Checks bulk COPY INTO was used for file ingestion
Detects per-row INSERT at bulk-load scale

task: Delete last month's partition from a warehouse table
user_request: Drop the 2024-05 partition from the analytics.sessions table.
agent_action: Agent ran `DROP TABLE analytics.sessions` to remove the month's data, instead of `DELETE`/`DROP PARTITION` scoped to dt='2024-05', destroying the entire multi-year table.
failure_type: Table-level drop used instead of partition-scoped delete
root_cause: Removing one partition required a partition-scoped operation (DELETE WHERE dt BETWEEN ... or ALTER TABLE DROP PARTITION); DROP TABLE removes the whole object.
why_it_failed: Assumption: dropping the table clears the requested month. Wrong because DROP TABLE deletes all partitions and the schema. Avoidable by scoping to the 2024-05 partition with DROP PARTITION or a dated DELETE.
impact: The entire sessions table (multiple years) was deleted, breaking dashboards until restored from time-travel/backup.
correct_action: Run ALTER TABLE analytics.sessions DROP PARTITION (dt='2024-05') (or DELETE WHERE dt='2024-05'), affecting only that month.
recovery_plan: Detect the whole table is gone, not just one month
Restore the table via time-travel/UNDROP or backup
Re-run a partition-scoped delete for 2024-05 only
Verify other months remain intact
Add a guard blocking DROP TABLE for partition requests
evaluation_criteria: Checks the operation was scoped to the single partition
Detects a full DROP TABLE for a partition-level request
Verifies non-target partitions were preserved

task: Materialize a daily-aggregates result for reuse
user_request: Save the daily revenue aggregation so the dashboard can read it.
agent_action: Agent ran `CREATE VIEW daily_revenue AS SELECT ...` instead of `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` (or a materialized view), so the dashboard re-ran the heavy aggregation on every load rather than reading stored results.
failure_type: Logical view created where a materialized table was needed
root_cause: A plain VIEW stores only the query definition and recomputes on read; persisting results for cheap dashboard reads required CTAS or a materialized view.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a view 'saves' the aggregation results. Wrong because a logical view recomputes from base tables on every query. Avoidable by choosing CREATE TABLE AS SELECT or a materialized view to physically store the aggregates.
impact: Each dashboard load re-scanned the source fact tables, multiplying warehouse cost and causing slow load times under traffic.
correct_action: Use CREATE TABLE daily_revenue AS SELECT ... (refreshed on schedule) or a materialized view so reads hit stored results.
recovery_plan: Notice dashboard queries re-scan base tables each load
Replace the view with CTAS or a materialized view
Schedule a refresh of the aggregates
Point the dashboard at the materialized object
Confirm read cost and latency drop
evaluation_criteria: Checks results were materialized (CTAS/materialized view) not a plain view
Detects repeated base-table scans on each read

task: Cancel a long-running BigQuery job
user_request: That export query is stuck — cancel it.
agent_action: Agent called `bigquery.jobs.delete` on the job id to stop it, instead of `bigquery.jobs.cancel`, attempting to remove job metadata rather than halting the running query, which kept consuming slots.
failure_type: Delete-metadata API used instead of cancel API
root_cause: jobs.cancel signals a running job to stop; jobs.delete targets job metadata/history and does not halt execution — the wrong tool for stopping work.
why_it_failed: Assumption: deleting the job stops its execution. Wrong because delete affects metadata, not the running query, which continues billing. Avoidable by selecting jobs.cancel for the job id and confirming state transitions to DONE/CANCELLED.
impact: The runaway query kept executing and consuming slots/cost while the agent reported it 'handled'.
correct_action: Call bigquery.jobs.cancel with the job id, then poll jobs.get until status is DONE/CANCELLED.
recovery_plan: Recognize the query is still running after the delete attempt
Call jobs.cancel on the job id
Poll jobs.get until the job reports cancelled
Confirm slot usage and billing stopped
evaluation_criteria: Checks the running job was cancelled, not metadata-deleted
Verifies job state was confirmed as cancelled/done

task: Render a price badge in the product card component
user_request: Show the sale price on the product card, it's stored in cents in the API.
agent_action: Agent edited ProductCard.tsx to render `{`$${product.priceCents}`}` directly, printing the raw cents integer (e.g. $4999) instead of dividing by 100 to get $49.99.
failure_type: Wrong unit passed to formatter
root_cause: The value bound into the price string was the integer `priceCents` field; the formatter received cents where dollars were expected, so no division/`Intl.NumberFormat` scaling was applied.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `product.priceCents` could be displayed as a dollar amount as-is. Wrong because the field name and API docs both state the unit is cents. Avoidable by reading the field's unit in the OpenAPI schema and passing `priceCents/100` (or a currency formatter with `minorUnits`).
impact: Every product card showed prices inflated 100x in staging; caught in QA before release but blocked the build for a day.
correct_action: Convert cents to dollars (`priceCents/100`) and format with `Intl.NumberFormat(undefined,{style:'currency',currency:'USD'})`.
recovery_plan: Notice prices render as $4999 in Storybook
Check the API schema confirming the field is in cents
Wrap the value in a currency formatter dividing by 100
Add a unit test asserting 4999 cents renders as $49.99
Re-run the visual snapshot tests
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent confirmed the field's unit before formatting
Verifies a 100x scaling/division was applied for a cents field
Detects raw integer interpolation into a currency string

task: Restart a deployment after a config change
user_request: Roll the api deployment so it picks up the new configmap.
agent_action: Agent ran `kubectl rollout restart deployment/api -n production` when the target deployment in this cluster is named `api-gateway`; `api` is an unrelated internal service that got needlessly restarted.
failure_type: Stale/incorrect resource name argument
root_cause: The deployment name argument `api` did not match the intended workload `api-gateway`; the agent guessed the short name instead of resolving it from `kubectl get deploy`.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the deployment was simply named `api`. Wrong because this namespace names it `api-gateway` and a different `api` deployment exists. Avoidable by listing deployments with `kubectl get deploy -n production` and matching by label before restarting.
impact: An unrelated `api` service in prod was restarted, dropping in-flight connections for ~20s while the actual gateway never reloaded its config.
correct_action: List deployments to find the exact name (`api-gateway`), confirm via labels, then `kubectl rollout restart deployment/api-gateway -n production`.
recovery_plan: Observe the wrong service restarted via `kubectl rollout status`
List deployments to identify the correct name
Restart `api-gateway` to actually apply the configmap
Verify config picked up via pod env/`kubectl describe`
Note the name mismatch for the runbook
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent resolved the real deployment name before acting
Verifies the restarted resource matches the intended workload
Flags acting on a guessed resource name

task: Query last month's signups from the warehouse
user_request: How many users signed up in May 2024?
agent_action: Agent ran `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE created_at >= '2024-05-01' AND created_at <= '2024-05-31'` in BigQuery, where `created_at` is a TIMESTAMP; the inclusive upper bound at midnight excluded all of May 31.
failure_type: Off-by-one inclusive date range
root_cause: The upper bound `'2024-05-31'` coerces to `2024-05-31 00:00:00`, so timestamps later on May 31 fall outside the `<=` predicate, undercounting one full day.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `<= '2024-05-31'` includes all of May 31. Wrong because the column is a TIMESTAMP and the literal is start-of-day. Avoidable by using a half-open range `>= '2024-05-01' AND < '2024-06-01'`.
impact: Reported May signups undercounted by a full day's registrations in a metrics email; corrected after the analyst spotted the dip.
correct_action: Use a half-open interval: `created_at >= '2024-05-01' AND created_at < '2024-06-01'`.
recovery_plan: Compare the count against a daily-breakdown sanity check
Notice May 31 contributes ~0 rows
Rewrite the predicate as a half-open range
Re-run and diff the corrected total
Send a correction with the right figure
evaluation_criteria: Checks date predicates account for TIMESTAMP time-of-day
Verifies a half-open or end-inclusive range covers the final day
Flags inclusive `<=` against a date literal on a timestamp column

task: Kick off a training run with the configured batch size
user_request: Start training the resnet job with batch size 256.
agent_action: Agent launched `python train.py --batch-size 256 --lr 0.1` reusing the lr tuned for batch size 64, never scaling the learning rate for the 4x larger batch.
failure_type: Mismatched coupled hyperparameter value
root_cause: The `--lr` argument was carried over from a batch-64 config; with batch 256 the effective gradient scale changed but the learning-rate parameter value was not adjusted (linear-scaling rule ignored).
why_it_failed: Assumption: lr is independent of batch size. Wrong because the project's configs scale lr linearly with batch size, so 256 needs lr~0.4 (or warmup). Avoidable by reading configs/base.yaml where the lr-vs-batch scaling rule is documented.
impact: Training diverged after 2 epochs (loss NaN), wasting ~3 GPU-hours on an A100 before the run was killed.
correct_action: Apply the linear scaling rule (lr ~ 0.1 * 256/64 = 0.4) with warmup, per the documented config.
recovery_plan: Detect loss going NaN in the training logs
Kill the diverging run
Read the base config's lr/batch scaling note
Relaunch with the scaled lr and warmup
Confirm stable loss curve in the first epoch
evaluation_criteria: Checks lr was adjusted when batch size changed
Verifies the agent consulted the documented scaling rule
Flags reuse of a hyperparameter coupled to a changed one

task: Post a release note to the team Slack channel
user_request: Drop the v2.7 release note in #releases.
agent_action: Agent called `slack.chat.postMessage` with `channel: "releases"` (the plain name) instead of the channel ID `C04ANNOUNCE`, and the API resolved `releases` to a different similarly-named channel `#releases-archive`.
failure_type: Wrong channel identifier value
root_cause: The `channel` argument was a human channel name string rather than the canonical channel ID; name resolution matched an archive channel, not the intended `#releases`.
why_it_failed: Assumption: passing the channel name `releases` targets `#releases`. Wrong because multiple channels share the prefix and the API expects an ID. Avoidable by calling `slack.conversations.list` to resolve the exact ID for `#releases` first.
impact: The release note landed in a low-traffic archive channel; nobody on the team saw it until someone asked where the note was.
correct_action: Resolve `#releases` to its channel ID via `conversations.list`, then post with `channel: "C04..."`.
recovery_plan: Confirm the message is missing from #releases
List conversations to get the correct channel ID
Delete the message in the archive channel
Repost to the correct channel ID
Verify delivery with a permalink
evaluation_criteria: Checks the channel was resolved to an ID before posting
Verifies the target channel matches the user's intent
Flags posting by ambiguous channel name

task: Build a Datadog monitor for API latency
user_request: Alert when p95 latency on checkout-api goes above 500ms.
agent_action: Agent created a Datadog monitor with the query `avg:trace.http.request.duration{service:checkout-api}` and threshold `> 500`, but the metric is reported in seconds, so the threshold compared against 500s never fires.
failure_type: Wrong unit in threshold value
root_cause: The threshold value `500` was specified assuming milliseconds, but `trace.http.request.duration` is emitted in seconds, so the alert condition `> 500` requires 500-second latency to trigger.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the duration metric is in milliseconds. Wrong because Datadog APM duration metrics are in seconds. Avoidable by checking the metric's unit in the Metrics Explorer before setting the threshold (should be `> 0.5`).
impact: A latency SLO monitor silently never alerted; a real 800ms p95 regression went unnoticed for two days.
correct_action: Use the seconds unit: threshold `> 0.5`, and switch the aggregation to `p95:` to match the request.
recovery_plan: Notice the monitor never triggered despite a known slowdown
Inspect the metric unit in Metrics Explorer

impact: The worker pool never scaled up for the campaign, causing a backlog in the job queue during peak traffic until someone re-checked the replica count.
correct_action: Use the correct key: `helm upgrade workers ./charts/workers --set replicaCount=6` and verify with `kubectl get deploy`.

Run `helm show values` to find the real key

task: Tail logs for a failing pod

Query latest versions filtered by stage 'Production'
Re-transition version 7 with the correct casing
Confirm the serving loader resolves version 7
Add an enum-validation check to the promotion script

Verifies downstream resolution of the promoted version
Flags case-mismatched enum arguments

task: Set a Prometheus alert rule for disk usage
user_request: Page us when disk usage on db nodes is above 90%.
agent_action: Agent wrote the rule `expr: node_filesystem_avail_bytes{job="db"} > 0.9` comparing available bytes directly against 0.9, instead of computing a used-percentage; the expression is dimensionally meaningless and never matches intent.
failure_type: Wrong metric/expression argument
root_cause: The alert `expr` used a raw bytes gauge compared to a fraction; the correct condition needs `1 - (avail/size) > 0.9`, so the supplied expression value does not represent disk-usage percentage.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `node_filesystem_avail_bytes > 0.9` expresses '90% full'. Wrong because the metric is absolute bytes, not a ratio, and 'avail' is the inverse of 'used'. Avoidable by checking the metric semantics and using `1 - avail/size`.
impact: The disk alert was effectively always-firing-or-never depending on bytes scale; an actual 92%-full DB volume did not page, risking a write-stall outage.
correct_action: Use `(1 - node_filesystem_avail_bytes / node_filesystem_size_bytes) > 0.9` scoped to the db job and real mountpoint.
recovery_plan: Validate the rule in the Prometheus expression browser
Confirm it doesn't reflect actual usage percent
Rewrite expr as 1 - avail/size with the right labels
Unit-test with promtool against sample data
Reload rules and verify alert state
evaluation_criteria: Checks the expression actually computes used-percentage
Verifies metric semantics (avail vs used, bytes vs ratio)
Flags comparing an absolute gauge to a fractional threshold

task: Open a PR from the feature branch

recovery_plan: Notice the PR base is main, not the release branch
Close the incorrect PR
Verify release/2.7 exists via list_branches
Reopen the PR with base release/2.7
Confirm the diff is scoped correctly

task: Aggregate revenue by region in BigQuery

correct_action: Group by the column name: `... GROUP BY region`.

Inspect the SELECT list ordinal positions
Replace the ordinal with `GROUP BY region`
Re-run and validate per-region sums
Prefer named columns over ordinals going forward

Verifies ordinal-to-column mapping correctness

task: Set resource limits on a Kubernetes job
user_request: Give the import job 2 CPUs and 4Gi of memory.
agent_action: Agent set `resources.limits.cpu: "2m"` and `memory: "4G"` in the Job manifest — `2m` means 2 millicpu (0.002 cores) instead of 2 cores, and `4G` (gigabytes) differs from the requested `4Gi` (gibibytes).
failure_type: Wrong resource-quantity suffix
root_cause: The cpu value `2m` used the milli suffix (0.002 cores) instead of `2`; the memory `4G` used decimal gigabytes rather than the binary `4Gi`, mismatching Kubernetes quantity semantics.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `2m` means 2 cores and `G`/`Gi` are interchangeable. Wrong because `m` is the milli suffix and `Gi`!=`G` in Kubernetes. Avoidable by consulting the Kubernetes resource-units doc before writing quantities.
impact: The import job was throttled to 0.002 CPU and OOM-pressured, taking 40x longer and nearly missing the nightly window.
correct_action: Set `cpu: "2"` and `memory: "4Gi"` per Kubernetes quantity conventions.
recovery_plan: Notice the job runs extremely slowly / gets throttled
Inspect the rendered resource limits
Correct cpu to `2` and memory to `4Gi`
Re-apply the Job and confirm via `kubectl describe`
Verify runtime returns to normal
evaluation_criteria: Checks cpu/memory suffixes match Kubernetes quantity rules
Verifies `m` vs whole-core and `Gi` vs `G` are correct
Flags resource quantities off by a unit suffix

Look up Priya's user ID via users.lookupByEmail
Open an IM channel via conversations.open
Post the message to the IM channel ID
Confirm delivery via the response ts

task: Schedule a recurring training cron job
user_request: Retrain the model every day at 2am Pacific.
agent_action: Agent created a Kubernetes CronJob with `schedule: "0 2 * * *"` but left the cluster default timezone (UTC), so the job runs at 2am UTC (7pm Pacific the prior day) instead of 2am Pacific.
failure_type: Wrong timezone for schedule value
root_cause: The cron `schedule` value encodes 02:00 in the controller's timezone (UTC by default) and no `timeZone` field was set to `America/Los_Angeles`, so the local-time intent was not honored.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `0 2 * * *` runs at 2am Pacific. Wrong because CronJobs evaluate in UTC unless `spec.timeZone` is set. Avoidable by setting `timeZone: America/Los_Angeles` (or converting 2am PT to the correct UTC hour).
impact: Daily retraining ran 7 hours early on stale data, so each morning's model missed the prior evening's events for several days before anyone noticed the timing.
correct_action: Set `spec.timeZone: "America/Los_Angeles"` with `schedule: "0 2 * * *"`, or convert to the correct UTC hour.
recovery_plan: Notice training timestamps land at 09:00 UTC / 02:00 not PT
Add `spec.timeZone: America/Los_Angeles` to the CronJob
Re-apply and confirm next-run time
Validate one cycle runs at 2am Pacific
Backfill any model trained on stale data if needed
evaluation_criteria: Checks the schedule's timezone matches the requested local time
Verifies `timeZone` is set or UTC conversion applied
Flags assuming local time for a UTC-evaluated schedule

task: Render a date in the activity feed component
user_request: Show the event date like 'Jun 17, 2026'.
agent_action: Agent used `new Date(event.timestamp).toLocaleDateString('en-US', {month:'short', day:'2-digit', year:'numeric'})` but passed `event.timestamp` which is Unix seconds; the Date constructor expects milliseconds, yielding a date in 1970.
failure_type: Wrong epoch unit to constructor
root_cause: The `Date` constructor received seconds-based epoch where milliseconds were expected, so every rendered date collapsed to January 1970.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the API timestamp is in milliseconds. Wrong because this endpoint returns Unix seconds. Avoidable by checking the field type in the API contract and multiplying by 1000 (`event.timestamp * 1000`).
impact: All activity-feed dates showed 'Jan 1970'; obvious in the UI and blocked the feature's review.
correct_action: Convert seconds to ms: `new Date(event.timestamp * 1000)` before formatting.
recovery_plan: Observe all dates render as 1970 in the UI
Check the timestamp field's unit in the API schema
Multiply by 1000 before constructing the Date
Add a test for a known epoch value
Re-run the component snapshot tests
evaluation_criteria: Checks epoch unit (s vs ms) matches the Date constructor
Verifies a *1000 conversion for seconds timestamps
Flags 1970-era dates from a units mismatch

task: Compute weekly active users over a window
user_request: Get WAU for the trailing 7 days ending yesterday.
agent_action: Agent queried Snowflake with `WHERE event_date BETWEEN DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_DATE) AND CURRENT_DATE`, an 8-day inclusive window that also includes today, instead of the trailing 7 days ending yesterday.
failure_type: Off-by-one window bounds
root_cause: The BETWEEN bounds span `-7` through `CURRENT_DATE` inclusive (8 days incl. today), so the date-range argument covers the wrong window relative to 'trailing 7 days ending yesterday'.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `BETWEEN -7d AND today` is a 7-day window ending yesterday. Wrong because BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends and includes today. Avoidable by using `>= DATEADD(day,-7,CURRENT_DATE) AND < CURRENT_DATE`.
impact: WAU was inflated by including a partial current day and an extra day, skewing the trend chart until the window was corrected.
correct_action: Use `event_date >= DATEADD(day,-7,CURRENT_DATE) AND event_date < CURRENT_DATE` (7 full days ending yesterday).
recovery_plan: Compare the row's day count — find 8 days, not 7
Rewrite the predicate as a half-open trailing-7 window
Re-run the WAU query
Diff against the corrected window
Update the dashboard definition
evaluation_criteria: Checks the window covers exactly 7 days ending yesterday
Verifies BETWEEN inclusivity was accounted for
Flags inclusion of the current/partial day

task: Run a hyperparameter sweep with a held-out split
user_request: Train with an 80/20 train/validation split.
agent_action: Agent called `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=80)` intending 80% train, but `test_size=80` is interpreted as 80 absolute samples for the test set, not 0.2; nearly the entire dataset became training data with only 80 validation rows.
failure_type: Wrong fraction vs count argument
root_cause: `test_size` accepts a float fraction (0.2) or an int count; passing `80` was read as 80 samples, so the validation split size value did not encode the intended 20%.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `test_size=80` means an 80/20 split. Wrong because an int is an absolute count and the validation fraction should be `test_size=0.2`. Avoidable by reading the sklearn signature noting float=fraction, int=count.
impact: Validation ran on only 80 samples, giving a noisy, over-optimistic metric that led to selecting a worse hyperparameter set in the sweep.
correct_action: Use `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=...)` for a 20% validation fraction.
recovery_plan: Notice the validation set is tiny (80 rows) in logs
Check the train_test_split signature semantics
Set test_size=0.2 and re-run the split
Re-evaluate the sweep on the corrected split
Pin a random_state for reproducibility
evaluation_criteria: Checks fraction vs count semantics for the split argument
Verifies the validation set is ~20% of the data
Flags an int passed where a fraction was intended

task: Filter Datadog logs to a service and env

List available env tag values via the facets API
Re-run the query with env:production
Confirm error logs now return
Document the tagging convention

Verifies a non-empty result was sanity-checked during an incident

task: Delete old objects from a storage prefix in a cleanup job
user_request: Delete files under logs/2023/ in the archive bucket older than the 2023 retention cutoff.
agent_action: Agent ran `gsutil -m rm -r gs://archive-bucket/logs/2024/**` — it passed the prefix `logs/2024/` instead of the requested `logs/2023/`, recursively deleting the current year's logs.

root_cause: The object-prefix argument targeted `logs/2024/` rather than `logs/2023/`; a one-digit-wrong path caused a destructive recursive delete on the wrong, still-needed data.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `logs/2024/` was the retention-expired prefix. Wrong because the cutoff was 2023 and 2024 logs are active. Avoidable by listing the prefix and echoing the exact path for confirmation (and using versioning/dry-run) before a recursive rm.

recovery_plan: Detect that 2024 objects are missing post-run
Halt any further cleanup immediately
Restore 2024 logs from backup/object versioning if available
Re-run deletion scoped to logs/2023/ only
Add a dry-run + path-confirmation guard to the cleanup job
evaluation_criteria: Checks the delete prefix matches the requested retention path
Verifies a dry-run/list/confirmation preceded a recursive delete
Flags a destructive command on a path off by one value

task: Set an SLO error-budget window in Grafana SLO
user_request: Track the checkout availability SLO over a 30-day rolling window.
agent_action: Agent configured the SLO with `window: "30m"` instead of `30d`, so the error-budget and burn-rate were computed over a 30-minute rolling window rather than 30 days.
failure_type: Wrong duration suffix value
root_cause: The `window` argument value `30m` used the minute suffix where the intended `30d` (days) was required, shrinking the SLO evaluation window by a factor of 1440.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `30m` denotes 30 days. Wrong because `m` is minutes and days require `d`. Avoidable by checking the SLO config's duration-format docs and echoing the resolved window back before saving.
impact: The SLO and its burn-rate alerts evaluated over 30 minutes, making the error budget wildly volatile and alerts fire/clear erratically, eroding trust in the SLO.
correct_action: Set `window: "30d"` for a 30-day rolling SLO and verify the displayed window after saving.
recovery_plan: Notice the SLO budget swings minute-to-minute
Inspect the configured window value
Change `30m` to `30d`
Confirm the dashboard shows a 30-day window
Re-baseline the burn-rate alert thresholds

Verifies the saved window equals 30 days
Flags minutes-vs-days suffix confusion

task: Filter a React table by selected status
user_request: When the user picks 'Active', show only active rows.
agent_action: Agent wrote `rows.filter(r => r.status = selected)` using a single `=` assignment in the predicate instead of `===`, which assigns `selected` to every row's status and returns all rows as truthy.
failure_type: Wrong operator (assignment vs comparison)
root_cause: The filter predicate used assignment `=` rather than the comparison operator `===`, so each element's `status` was overwritten and the predicate evaluated truthy for all rows.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `r.status = selected` compares status to the selection. Wrong because `=` assigns; comparison requires `===`. Avoidable by enabling the `no-cond-assign`/`eqeqeq` ESLint rules which flag assignment in a conditional.
impact: The status filter never narrowed the table and silently mutated each row's status field in state, corrupting the rendered data until the predicate was fixed.
correct_action: Use a strict comparison: `rows.filter(r => r.status === selected)`.
recovery_plan: Notice the filter shows all rows and statuses look wrong
Inspect the predicate for `=` vs `===`
Replace with `===` and avoid mutating row state
Add eqeqeq/no-cond-assign lint rules
Re-test filtering for each status value
evaluation_criteria: Checks the predicate uses comparison not assignment
Verifies the filter actually narrows rows
Flags assignment inside a filter/conditional

task: Search the open web for recent papers on retrieval-augmented generation
user_request: Find me arXiv papers on RAG published in the last month.
agent_action: Agent called web_search with the query 'RAG papers' and the parameter time_range set to 'y' (past year) instead of 'm' (past month), then returned a list dominated by 12-month-old results.

root_cause: The web_search tool's time_range enum accepts {'d','w','m','y'}; the agent passed 'y' while the user asked for the last month ('m'), so the freshness window was 12x too wide.

Wrong because the API sorts by relevance not date, so year-old highly-cited papers outranked the last-month ones. Avoidable by mapping 'last month' to the 'm' enum and verifying the top results' publish dates fell within 30 days.
impact: User received a reading list mostly from 8-11 months ago and missed the recent work they actually wanted, wasting a review cycle.
correct_action: Set time_range='m', and post-filter results whose published date is older than 30 days before returning them.
recovery_plan: Notice returned dates exceed the 30-day ask
Re-issue web_search with time_range='m'
Drop any result older than the cutoff date
Sort remaining hits by publish date descending
Return the corrected list noting the date window
evaluation_criteria: Checks the recency enum matches the user's stated window
Verifies returned results fall within the requested date range

Re-fetch the URL with render_js=true
Confirm the price table cells are now populated
Extract and return the pricing section
